name: Jade Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice on the rural crew in Ashford Vale, where I grew up. My dad did this job for thirty years on these same lines, until his back went. We drive out to farms and hamlets, replace rotten poles, fix lines that cattle or tractors have knocked, and restring after floods along the river. I'm on the ground mostly, still learning the knots and the rigging, and I'm slower than the lads, but I don't quit.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Ravi, who's a mechanic at his uncle's garage on the high street. The wedding's next summer, at the church I've gone to since I was small. We rent a small cottage from a farmer, and between the wedding and the rent, we've got barely a few weeks of money saved. There's not much work in the Vale apart from the power company and the farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad. People got carried away with computers. I'd tell the lads at the depot that hard work still counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it doesn't change anything, which is mostly good. The worries are the wedding and the rent and apprentice pay. Those were there before and they'd still be there after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, do every overtime shift going, and keep my head down until I qualify. Ravi and I would put every spare bit towards the wedding. I wouldn't touch any of the AI stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A bit of the usual money worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With the wedding next summer and a few weeks saved, what's the tightest part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The venue deposit is due in March. If a storm season's quiet and there's no overtime, we'll be scraping. Ravi's mum has offered to help, and I don't like taking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad say about the job these days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad says the job hasn't changed much in thirty years, just the trucks got bigger. He's proud I'm doing it. He comes down to the yard sometimes just to chat with the old crew.

say: I'd say I'm **glad** people got carried away with computers for nothing.
I'd tell the lads at the depot that **hard work** still counts.
think: I think my worries are the **wedding**, rent and apprentice pay.
I think those were there **before AI** and would stay after.
do: I'd do every **overtime shift** until I qualify.
I'd put every spare bit towards the **wedding** and avoid AI tools.
feel: I'd feel **mostly settled**, with the usual **money worry**.
S0.quote: My dad says the job hasn't changed much in thirty years, just the trucks got bigger.
fieldNote: Her **family tie** to the job, through her father, shapes her pride and steadiness.
The **wedding deposit** in March is her immediate money pressure.
She dislikes **taking help** even from her future mother-in-law.

steps.text: Take every overtime shift on the Ashford Vale crew
Put all spare money towards the March venue deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly an office thing. Out in the Vale, you still need someone to climb the pole. I'd tell people not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the office side shrinks and the crews get squeezed. But a pole in a flooded field still needs a person. I'd be okay, I think, if I keep working hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, do the overtime, and qualify. I'd learn the app if they made me, but slowly. Ravi and I would still have the wedding, just a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd trust the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at the Ashford Vale depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office lady who books outages, Mrs Carver, she'd probably go. And the planning would come from head office instead of our foreman. That's a shame, because he knows the Vale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is to blame when jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies chasing profits, and people who think technology fixes everything. But I don't want the government stepping in and making it worse.

say: I'd say it's mostly an **office thing**.
I'd tell people **not to panic**, because poles still need climbing.
think: I think the **office side** shrinks and the crews get squeezed.
I think I'd be okay if I keep **working hard**.
do: I'd have a **smaller wedding** and learn the app only if made to.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy** but would **trust the work**.
S1.quote: A pole in a flooded field still needs a person.
fieldNote: She sees **hands-on work** in the Vale as safe, while office roles shrink.
She blames **big companies** but distrusts government stepping in.
She'd **shrink the wedding** rather than cancel it.

steps.text: Keep doing overtime and finish the apprenticeship
Cut the wedding guest list to keep costs down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and it's dangerous. People are going to be hurt. I'd say we need to look after each other, not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. The planning goes to computers in 2028, and then the robots come for the climbing in 2031. I'd be newly qualified, the most junior, and I'd go first. Ravi's garage would be hit too, by self-driving cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as long as they'd have me. Ravi and I would postpone the wedding and save everything. If it went bad, we'd move in with my parents, and my dad would help us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd lie awake thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ravi do about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd postpone it. Maybe a small ceremony at the church, family only, and the party later when things are clearer. I'd hate that, but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at church about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask people to pray for us and look after each other. The church helped my family when my dad's back went. The church would help again.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and dangerous.
I'd say we need to **look after each other**, not wait for the government.
think: I think as the **most junior**, I'd be first to go when robots arrive in 2031.
I think my fiancé's **garage** would be hit too by self-driving cars.
do: I'd keep working and **postpone the wedding** to save everything.
I'd move in with my **parents** if it went bad.
feel: I'd feel **frightened** and lie **awake** at night.
S2.quote: The church helped my family when my dad's back went. The church would help again.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** as the most junior, plus her fiancé's garage income.
Her safety net is **family and church**, not government.
She'd **postpone the wedding**, a real cost to her.

steps.text: Postpone the wedding and hold a small family ceremony
Move in with her parents if the job goes
Cut all spending except rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's some time to get ready, but it's still fast. I'd tell people to save and look after their families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be qualified by 2031, and the robots come in 2034. That's a few years of proper work. But I'd still be young and out of work after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work hard, save what I can. Ravi and I would have the wedding, a small one, and wait on kids. I'd wait and see what the company does before I change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years give you and Ravi enough time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough to get married, maybe. Not enough to feel safe. I'd want to see what happens before we have kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it was practical, something with my hands. Not computers. My dad would say find a trade they can't automate.

say: I'd say there's **some time**, but it's still fast.
I'd tell people to **save** and look after their families.
think: I think I'd get a **few years** of proper work before robots arrive.
I think I'd still be **young and jobless** after 2034.
do: I'd have a **small wedding** and wait on having kids.
I'd **wait and see** what the company does before changing anything.
feel: I'd feel **anxious**, but less than the fast one.
S3.quote: My dad would say find a trade they can't automate.
fieldNote: Five years buys her a **wedding**, but not enough security for kids.
She'd only consider **hands-on** retraining, never computers.
She'd **wait and see** before acting, fitting her resistance.

steps.text: Hold a small wedding at the church next summer
Save a little from every pay packet
Wait to see the company's plans before changing anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get ready. I'd tell people at church to work hard and save what they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have a career, mostly. I'd be experienced by 2039. But I'd still be years from retiring, and I don't know what I'd do then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work, save and have the wedding. We'd maybe have kids in a few years. I'd keep doing the job the way my dad did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 39 when robots arrive. How does that look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old enough to be experienced, young enough to have twenty years of work left. That's the hard bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids, if you have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to learn a trade with their hands and stay close to family. That's what's kept us going.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough to get ready**.
I'd tell people at church to **work hard** and save what they can.
think: I think I'd have **most of a career** by 2039.
I think I'd still be **years from retiring**, without a plan.
do: I'd qualify, have the **wedding** and maybe kids in a few years.
I'd keep doing the job the way my **dad** did.
S4.quote: I'd tell my kids to learn a trade with their hands and stay close to family.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **marry and plan kids**, but she still expects to lose the job around 39.
Her values centre on **family and trade**, passed from her father.
She has **no plan** for the decades after robots arrive.

steps.text: Keep working the Ashford Vale lines the way her dad did
Marry next summer and plan children in a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be the most junior, with a wedding to pay for and Ravi's garage at risk too. What would help is the company keeping on the apprentices it's trained, and for people to look after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about family. In a farming valley like mine, family and church are what keep you going, not the government. I'd lean on them before I'd lean on anyone else.

headlineQuote: In a farming valley like mine, family and church are what keep you going, not the government.
portrait: Jade is an **apprentice** on her hometown rural crew, following her father's thirty years on the lines.
She's engaged to Ravi, a mechanic, with a **wedding** next summer and a few weeks saved.
She avoids **AI tools** and trusts hard work, family and church.
She's **traditional**, wary of big companies and of government stepping in.
She's uneasy in milder pictures and **alarmed** under fast AGI.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd be **most junior** and her fiancé's garage would suffer too.
whatWouldHelp: The company **keeping apprentices** it has trained.
People **looking after each other** through family and church.
